study.title: Linear-time sorts: counting, radix, bucket
study.locator: Three preconditions, three algorithms; Counting sort
study.depth: Skim LSD radix sort and Bucket sort for their preconditions only (fixed-width keys; near-uniform keys). Only counting sort is implemented here.

focus: Stability means equal keys keep their input order. Merge sort is stable because the merge emits the left run on ties (<=, not <). Quicksort and heap sort are not stable.

The merge recurrence \(T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)\) gives \(\Theta(n \log n)\) in the best, average and worst case. The shared buffer costs \(\Theta(n)\) extra space plus \(\Theta(\log n)\) stack; the already-sorted short-circuit recovers \(\Theta(n)\) on sorted input.

The lower bound counts leaves: \(n\) distinct keys admit \(n!\) permutations, so a decision tree needs height at least \(\lg(n!)\), which is \(\Omega(n \log n)\) by Stirling. It binds only comparison sorts on general input; counting sort never compares and needs bounded integer keys instead.

Equal asymptotics do not mean equal speed in Python. On a 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K with Python 3.13.14, a pure-Python merge sort on 20,000 random ints took 0.018 s against 0.0017 s for list.sort, about 10x. State the CPU and version with every timing you report.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement top-down merge sort with one shared auxiliary buffer, midpoint lo + (hi - lo)//2, <= in the merge, and the already-sorted short-circuit. On [5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 2, 6] it must return [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Stability check: [(5, 'a'), (3, 'b'), (5, 'c')] must come back [(3, 'b'), (5, 'a'), (5, 'c')]. Then run a Hypothesis differential test against sorted on 300 lists up to length 60 with seed 0.
traps: Using < instead of <= in the merge. Ties taken from the right run break stability silently while every sortedness test still passes.
Allocating a fresh auxiliary list in every merge call. Allocate once at the top; per-call allocation adds a hidden linear factor at each of the \(\log n\) levels.
Reading the lower bound as a ban on fast sorting. It bans fast comparison sorting on general input; bounded keys (counting) or fixed-width keys (radix) change the model and the bound does not apply.

selfTest.q: Prove that any comparison sort needs \(\Omega(n \log n)\) comparisons in the worst case.
selfTest.a: Model the sort as a decision tree: each internal node is one comparison and each leaf is one output permutation. Sorting \(n\) distinct keys needs at least \(n!\) leaves. A binary tree with \(L\) leaves has height at least \(\lg L\), so the height is at least \(\lg(n!)\). By Stirling, \(n! > (n/e)^n\), so \(\lg(n!) > n \lg n - n \lg e = \Omega(n \log n)\).

selfTest.q: Why does counting sort not contradict that bound?
selfTest.a: The bound counts comparisons on general input. Counting sort never compares keys; it indexes by key value, which needs bounded integer keys with \(k = O(n)\) for linear time. Change the assumption and the bound does not apply.

selfTest.q: Is Python's list.sort stable, and how do you check from a REPL?
selfTest.a: Yes, it is Timsort and stable. Check sorted([(5, 'a'), (3, 'b'), (5, 'c')], key=lambda p: p[0]): the two 5s keep the order ('a') before ('c').

selfTest.q: Why does merge sort cost \(\Theta(n \log n)\) even on already-sorted input without the short-circuit?
selfTest.a: Every level still visits all \(n\) elements to merge, and there are about \(\log_2 n\) levels regardless of order. The short-circuit only skips the merge work when the two runs are already ordered, which recovers \(\Theta(n)\) on sorted input.

study.title: Quickselect vs heap for top-K
study.locator: The decision; Algorithms compared; Side-by-side; Common misconceptions

focus: Lomuto invariant: at every scan step, arr[lo..i] holds elements <= pivot, arr[i+1..j-1] holds elements > pivot, and arr[j..hi-1] is unexamined. The final swap puts the pivot at its final sorted index. Median-of-three places the pivot at arr[hi]; that placement is part of the contract.

With the handbook's <= in the scan, keys equal to the pivot join the left band; Erickson's strict < sends them right. Either way all-equal input puts every key on one side, so Lomuto degenerates to \(\Theta(n^2)\) even with a random pivot. Three-way (Dutch flag) partition groups equal keys in one pass and recovers \(\Theta(n)\).
Random pivot is the correctness fix, not an optimization: a fixed last-element pivot is \(\Theta(n^2)\) on sorted input. Judges include large sorted and duplicate-heavy arrays, so test both yourself.

Top-k routing: a stream or tiny \(k\) favors a size-k heap (\(O(n \log k)\) time, \(O(k)\) space, no mutation); a whole array in memory with unsorted output favors quickselect (expected \(O(n)\)); sorted output adds \(O(k \log k)\). In CPython, heapq.nlargest runs in C: on a 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900K with Python 3.13.14 it took about 1.3 ms against about 6 ms for an in-place pure-Python quickselect on 100,000 ints with \(k = 100\), so count comparisons and wall-clock time separately.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement Lomuto partition with a random pivot swap and iterative quickselect for kth largest. Assert the post-condition on every partition call (pivot at its final index, everything left of it <= pivot, everything right of it > pivot). quickselect([3,2,1,5,6,4], 2) must return 5. Run a Hypothesis differential test against sorted on 300 lists up to length 40, including sorted and all-equal inputs, then add a three-way partition and time both on 10,000 equal keys.
traps: Converting \(k\) wrong: kth largest wants target index \(n-k\), kth smallest wants \(k-1\). For \(n=6\), \(k=2\), the target index is 4.
Quickselect mutates the caller's array. Copy at the boundary when the caller needs the input intact.
Recursing into the wrong side after partition. The pivot sits at its final sorted position; only the side containing the target index is read again. The rest is partitioned, not sorted.

selfTest.q: State the Lomuto invariant and what the final swap establishes.
selfTest.a: During the scan, arr[lo..i] holds elements <= pivot, arr[i+1..j-1] holds elements > pivot, and arr[j..hi-1] is unexamined. The final swap moves the pivot just past the <= band, so it sits at its final sorted index with everything left <= it and everything right > it.

selfTest.q: Why does Lomuto with a random pivot still go quadratic on all-equal input, and what fixes it?
selfTest.a: Every key equal to the pivot lands on one side (left with <=, right with <), so each partition removes only the pivot and \(T(n) = T(n-1) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n^2)\). Three-way partition groups all pivot-equal keys in one pass, so the recursion skips them and the cost is \(\Theta(n)\).

selfTest.q: When does a size-k heap beat quickselect for top-k, and when does it lose asymptotically?
selfTest.a: The heap wins when the input streams (quickselect needs random access to the whole array) or when \(O(k)\) space without mutation matters. At \(k = n/2\) the heap costs \(O(n \log n)\) and loses its edge while quickselect stays expected \(O(n)\). Sorted output adds \(O(k \log k)\) on top of either.

selfTest.q: What does introselect change about quickselect's worst case?
selfTest.a: It watches the recursion depth and switches to a guaranteed method past about \(2 \lg n\) levels: median-of-medians in Musser's design, which keeps the worst case linear, or heap selection in libstdc++'s nth_element, which caps it at \(O(n \log n)\). The median-of-medians proof belongs to algorithms/decomposition-greedy-randomness/divide-conquer-recurrences.

study.title: Algorithmica: Binary Search
study.locator: Binary Search (The Bottleneck); Removing Branches
study.depth: Read for the branch-prediction and cache explanation only. Every speedup number there (2.5x to 3x branchless on small arrays, about 2x Eytzinger against std::lower_bound) is a C++ measurement with Clang 10 on Zen 2; do not transfer any crossover point to Python.

focus: Closed [lo,hi] pairs with while lo <= hi and hi=mid-1; half-open [lo,hi) pairs with while lo < hi and hi=mid. Mixing the pairs is the non-termination bug.
lower_bound keeps equality right with nums[mid] < target; upper_bound keeps equality left with nums[mid] <= target. Their difference counts duplicates.
Answer-space search is Template C with a monotone predicate: feasibility must hold above (or below) a threshold with no gaps. Cost is \(O(F \log W)\) for predicate cost \(F\) and width \(W\).

Algorithmica's C++ numbers explain why equal-asymptotic searches cross over (an unpredictable branch costs 10 to 15 cycles, a cache miss up to 300), but Python's interpreter overhead moves every crossover. Verify bounds against bisect, not against ported constants.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement lower_bound, upper_bound and a first-true search on [lo,hi). On [1,2,2,2,3] with target 2, return 1 and 4. Reproduce Koko: piles [3,6,7,11] with h=8 must return 4. Run a Hypothesis differential test of both bounds against bisect_left and bisect_right on 300 sorted lists up to length 30.
traps: Returning lo for every template. The upper-bound twin and Template A need their own return values; derive each from the invariant instead of memorizing one.
Writing lo=mid or hi=mid in Template A after a miss. The closed interval needs mid+1 and mid-1 to shrink; the half-open forms are the ones that keep mid.
Searching on a predicate that is not monotone. Prove hours(k) is nonincreasing in \(k\) (or your predicate's direction) before trusting the loop; a gap in feasibility silently returns a wrong answer.

selfTest.q: Prove Template B terminates with lo at the lower bound.
selfTest.a: Invariant: every index j < lo has nums[j] < target and every index k >= hi has nums[k] >= target. Each iteration replaces [lo,hi) with a strictly smaller interval that preserves the invariant, since mid sits strictly inside while lo < hi. The width reaches zero, so lo == hi, and the invariant says every index below lo is < target and every index from lo on is >= target (lo = n when none is), so lo is the lower bound.

selfTest.q: On [1,2,2,2,3], what do exact-match search, lower_bound and upper_bound return for target 2, and why?
selfTest.a: Exact match returns some index in {1,2,3}. lower_bound returns 1 because the strict comparison keeps equality right; upper_bound returns 4 because the non-strict comparison keeps equality left. The duplicate count is 4 - 1 = 3.

selfTest.q: Why is binary search correct on the Koko predicate when speeds are not stored in an array?
selfTest.a: hours(k) is nonincreasing in \(k\): a faster speed never needs more hours. That monotonicity is the only requirement; the loop searches the predicate, not a sorted array. Each probe scans \(n\) piles, so the cost is \(O(n \log \max(piles))\).

selfTest.q: A colleague ports Algorithmica's branchless binary search to Python expecting 2.5x. What do you tell them?
selfTest.a: The 2.5x to 3x number is Algorithmica's C++ measurement (Clang 10, Zen 2) on small arrays. Python's per-iteration interpreter overhead dominates and removes the branch-prediction effect, so the constant does not transfer. Measure with timeit on the real workload instead.

study.title: Level-order traversal: BFS on trees
study.locator: The trigger; The pattern; What changes between the variants; Two pitfalls that bite

focus: Height convention used here: height(null) = 0 and a leaf has height 1 (nodes on the path). The AVL chapter switches to edges; never mix the two conventions in one argument.
Iterative inorder keeps every ancestor whose left subtree is done but whose value is unemitted; after emitting, move to cur.right, not None.
Level order needs the level_size = len(queue) snapshot taken once per level. Reading the queue length inside the inner loop merges levels.

CPython's default recursion limit is 1000 (check with sys.getrecursionlimit), so a recursive traversal fails on a skewed tree of a few thousand nodes while a balanced tree of 100,000 nodes (depth about 17) is fine. The iterative forms have no such cap.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement iterative inorder and level-order with the snapshot line. On the chapter's canonical tree (preorder [1,2,4,5,3,6], inorder [4,2,5,1,3,6]), return inorder [4,2,5,1,3,6] and level order [[1],[2,3],[4,5,6]]. Check both against recursive versions on 200 random BSTs up to 25 nodes with fixed seeds, plus empty, single-node and skewed inputs.
traps: Pushing the left child before the right in iterative preorder. Push right first so the left child pops next.
Serializing without null markers. Preorder [2,1] fits two different trees; markers disambiguate.
Using list.pop(0) as the BFS queue. Each pop costs \(O(n)\), which makes level order \(O(n^2)\); use collections.deque.

selfTest.q: Why does inorder traversal of a BST emit sorted keys?
selfTest.a: Inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. Every key left of a node is smaller and every key right of it is larger, so induction on the tree gives ascending order. This needs the BST invariant and is false for general binary trees.

selfTest.q: What breaks if the inner level-order loop reads len(queue) on every check instead of snapshotting?
selfTest.a: Children appended during the level change the bound mid-level, so the loop consumes the next level too and the boundaries merge. The snapshot fixes the count before any appends happen.

selfTest.q: Preorder [1,2] and postorder [2,1] fit more than one tree. Show the ambiguity and the fix.
selfTest.a: Both fit root 1 with a single child 2 on either side; the one-child direction is undetermined. Null markers (or an inorder sequence, which needs distinct keys) fix the shape.

selfTest.q: A recursive inorder fails on a skewed tree of 5,000 nodes but works on a balanced tree of 100,000. Why?
selfTest.a: Stack use follows depth, not size: skewed depth is \(n-1 = 4,999\) against the default limit of 1000, while balanced depth is about 17. The fix is the iterative form, or a deliberate limit raise.

focus: Bounded validation passes (lo,hi) down and checks lo < val < hi strictly. The tree [5,4,6,null,null,3,7] passes every child-only check, yet node 3 sits in the right subtree of 5 and fails the inherited bound.
Hibbard deletion copies the inorder successor's value, then deletes the successor, which has at most one child. Never rewire the successor object into the deleted slot; that loses the left subtree.

AVL dispatch asks two questions: which side is heavy (sign of the balance factor) and outer versus inner (sign agreement). Same sign rotates once; opposite signs rotate twice. Insert needs \(O(1)\) rotations because the subtree height returns to its old value.

Segment-tree query visits at most four vertices per level because only the two boundary vertices split; interior vertices exit on exact match. The min/max clipping plus the empty-range guard is what makes that proof work.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement BST insert, bounded validation and Hibbard delete. Insert [5,3,8,1,4,7,9] and assert inorder [1,3,4,5,7,8,9]; assert validation rejects [5,4,6,null,null,3,7] and LeetCode's [5,1,4,null,null,3,6]; delete 5 and assert inorder [1,3,4,7,8,9] with validation true. Implement a segment tree with point update and range sum: on [1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15], update index 3 to 6 and assert sumRange(2,5) is 31. Differential-test the segment tree against brute force on random arrays up to length 50.
traps: Using int sentinels (INT_MIN, INT_MAX) as initial bounds. A key equal to the sentinel breaks the check; use infinities, boxed nullable bounds or a wider type.
Deleting by rewiring instead of value copy, or forgetting to delete the successor copy afterwards. Both corrupt the ordering or duplicate a key.
Counting segment-tree vertices as \(2n-1\) and allocating \(2n\). When \(n\) is not a power of two the implicit layout overflows; allocate \(4n\).

selfTest.q: Show a tree that passes child-only BST checks but is not a BST, and state the check that rejects it.
selfTest.a: In [5,4,6,null,null,3,7], every parent is correctly ordered against its own children, but node 3 sits in the right subtree of 5. Bounded validation rejects it: node 3 inherits lo=5 and fails 5 < 3.

selfTest.q: Why does Hibbard deletion of a two-child node always terminate?
selfTest.a: It copies the inorder successor's value and recurses into the right subtree for the successor. The successor is the leftmost node there, so it has no left child and the recursion lands in the zero-child or right-only case at once.

selfTest.q: Derive the AVL height bound from the Fibonacci recurrence.
selfTest.a: A height-h AVL tree is smallest when its subtrees are minimal with heights \(h-1\) and \(h-2\), giving \(T(h) = T(h-1) + T(h-2) + 1\) with \(T(0)=0\) and \(T(1)=1\). That solves to \(F(h+2)-1\) nodes, so \(n \ge F(h+2)-1\) forces \(h \le 1.44 \log_2(n+2)\): about 44 percent worse than perfectly balanced.

selfTest.q: Why is a segment-tree range query \(O(\log n)\) rather than \(O(n)\)?
selfTest.a: At each level only the leftmost and rightmost visited vertices can straddle the query boundary and split; interior vertices match exactly and stop. That caps each level at four vertices over \(O(\log n)\) levels, with the empty-range guard absorbing the half-empty splits.

units.title: Heaps and priority queues
outcomes: Derive why bottom-up heap construction is linear while repeated insertion is \(\Theta(n \log n)\).
Implement sift-up, sift-down, Floyd build, push, pop and replace with invariant tests, using heapq only as an oracle.
Implement the two-heap streaming median and defend its size and ordering invariants.
units.why: Heaps buy priority operations in logarithmic time with plain array storage. The linear build and the two-heap median are the two derivations that recur everywhere else.

next.note: Return there for the top-k routing decision between heaps and quickselect.
Dijkstra consumes a priority queue with stale entries.

study.title: Heaps and priority queues
study.locator: What a heap actually is; The two primitives; The full operation table; Building a heap in linear time; Worked example: LC 295; Where readers go wrong
study.depth: Skim the LC 215 and LC 23 worked examples; kth-largest belongs to the quickselect unit and k-way merge is not assigned.

study.title: Two-heap median archetypes: when one heap is not enough
study.locator: Streaming median (two-heap balance invariant); Variants side-by-side
study.depth: Skip sliding-window median and the sketch survey; only the append-only variant is implemented here.

focus: Most nodes are leaves with short subtrees: level \(h\) holds about \(n/2^{h+1}\) nodes at \(O(h)\) sift cost each, and the series \((n/2)\) times sum \(h/2^h\) converges to \(O(n)\). Repeated insertion instead pays \(\log 1 + \ldots + \log n = \log(n!))\), which is \(\Theta(n \log n)\).

Floyd starts at n//2 - 1, the last internal node, and moves right to left so every sift-down sees valid child heaps. That order is the MAX-HEAPIFY precondition; building by sift-up throws the linear bound away.

Two-heap invariants: 0 <= len(lower) - len(upper) <= 1 with the extra element in lower, and max(lower) <= min(upper). Push-then-rotate maintains both with \(O(\log n)\) per insert and \(O(1)\) per query.

heapq is min-heap only and heapify runs in documented \(O(len(heap))\) time. Max-heap idioms negate keys, and payloads need a tiebreak slot (the LC 23 tuple trick) so equal priorities never compare task objects.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement Floyd max-heap build plus push and pop. With random.seed(0) and random.sample(range(10^6), 2000), assert the result is a valid max-heap holding the same multiset, and count comparisons (at most \(2n = 4000\)). Implement MedianFinder with the push-then-rotate rule: after add(1) and add(2) the median is 1.5; after add(3) it is 2.0. Differential-test both against heapq and brute-force medians on random streams.
traps: Calling sift-down on a node whose children are not heaps yet. The child-heaps precondition is load-bearing; Floyd's right-to-left order is what establishes it.
Rebalancing the two heaps in the wrong order. Push to lower, move its top to upper, then rotate back only if upper outgrew lower; skipping the last step breaks the size invariant on even totals.
Averaging the two middle values with // instead of /. Floor division truncates the even-case median (1.5 becomes 1).

selfTest.q: Prove Floyd's build is \(O(n)\).
selfTest.a: Nodes at height \(h\) number about \(n/2^{h+1}\) and each costs at most \(h\) sift steps. The total is at most \((n/2)\) times the sum of \(h/2^h\) over all \(h\), and that series converges to 2, giving at most about \(n\) sift steps and \(2n\) comparisons. Naive repeated insertion instead pays \(\log 1 + \ldots + \log n = \log(n!)\), which is \(\Theta(n \log n)\) by Stirling.

selfTest.q: Why must the build loop start at n//2 - 1 and go down?
selfTest.a: Indices [n//2, n) are leaves, which are trivially valid single-element heaps, so n//2 - 1 is the last internal node. Descending guarantees both children are already valid heaps when a node is sifted, which is the sift-down precondition.

selfTest.q: State both two-heap invariants and compute the median for odd and even totals.
selfTest.a: Size: lower holds at most one element more than upper, never fewer. Ordering: every lower key is at most every upper key. Odd total: the median is lower's root. Even total: the average of the two roots.

selfTest.q: heapq has no max-heap. How do you store (priority, task) pairs, and what breaks on ties?
selfTest.a: Push (-priority, index, task) with a tiebreak counter: negation flips the order and the counter keeps task objects uncompared. Without it, equal priorities fall through to comparing tasks, which raises TypeError for unordered types.

units.title: Tries and prefix lookup
outcomes: Explain trie representation, prefix lookup cost and memory cost, and when a trie beats hashing.
Implement a trie with insert, search, startsWith and wildcard search, tested on empty strings, duplicates and shared prefixes.
Route a prefix problem to a trie, a hash map or a sorted set from its query shape.
units.why: Tries trade key storage for shared prefixes. Prefix enumeration and constrained search are awkward in hash maps and slow in sorted sets.

next.note: Wildcard search is depth-first search over trie children; that unit owns the general backtracking form.
Prefix structure reappears in string dynamic programming.

study.title: Tries
study.locator: What's in the structure; What is_end is and is not; Choosing the children container; LC 211: wildcards and a tree-shaped walk; What it actually costs
study.depth: Skim LC 212 (the trie as prune oracle) and Pattern variants worth knowing for recognition; only LC 208 and 211 are implemented here.

focus: search checks is_end; startsWith does not. After inserting car and card, the node for car is terminal and still has a d child: terminal and leaf are orthogonal.

Lookup costs \(O(L)\) in the key length with one step per character, the same factor a hash pays to read the key. The trie wins on prefix queries (list every word under ca), which hashing cannot enumerate without scanning the table.
The children container sets the constants: a 26-array is \(O(1)\) per step but wastes nulls (the chapter estimates about 20 MB per 100k nodes); dict children handle Unicode and sparse alphabets.

Wildcard '.' tries every non-null child by DFS. LC 211 allows at most 2 dots, so the fan-out caps at \(26^2 = 676\) paths; with many dots, scanning the stored words of the query's length is the simpler bound.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement a trie with dict children. Insert apple and app; assert search(app) is True, search(appl) is False and startsWith(app) is True. Add wildcard search; assert wildcard('.pp') is True and wildcard('b..') is False. Differential-test search and startsWith against a Python set oracle on random word lists including empty strings and duplicates.
traps: Pasting search into startsWith. The shared walk must skip the is_end check for prefix queries.
Sizing the children array for lowercase only, then indexing ord('A') - ord('a') = -32. Dict children or explicit alphabet checks avoid the silent negative index.
Running one DFS per word on a board instead of one DFS guided by the trie. The trie prunes every word sharing an impossible prefix at once.

selfTest.q: After inserting car and card, is the node for car a leaf? Is it terminal?
selfTest.a: Terminal but not a leaf: is_end is True and it still has the d child. The two flags are independent.

selfTest.q: Why can a hash map not answer 'list every word starting with ca' efficiently?
selfTest.a: Hashes destroy prefix locality: matching words scatter across buckets, so enumeration scans the whole table. A trie walks to ca once, then enumerates only that subtree.

selfTest.q: What is the worst-case cost of wildcard search with \(k\) dots over alphabet size \(R\)?
selfTest.a: \(O(R^k)\) trie paths, since each dot fans out to every non-null child. LC 211 stays feasible by capping queries at 2 dots (\(26^2 = 676\)). With many dots, grouping words by length and scanning the group costs \(O(N L)\) for \(N\) words of length \(L\) and is the safer bound.

selfTest.q: When does a sorted set beat a trie for prefix queries?
selfTest.a: On memory and simplicity for a single range: bisecting 'ca' to 'cb' answers one prefix query with no per-node overhead. Tries win when many prefix walks share structure or when per-character steps with wildcards are needed.

units.title: Interval ordering, merging and sweep lines
outcomes: State the interval-merging invariant and implement merge and insert with edge tests for touching endpoints and containment.
Implement event sweeps with an explicit tie-break and defend the ends-before-starts versus starts-before-ends choice from the interval convention.
Solve unseen interval problems by reading the verb (collapse, insert, concurrency) and picking the matching running state.
units.why: Intervals turn sorting into scheduling. One sort plus one left-to-right walk answers merging, insertion and concurrency when the running state matches the question's verb.

next.note: Interval scheduling proofs build on the merging order established here.
Concurrency counting reuses the heap as its active set.

study.title: Merge intervals archetypes
study.locator: The decision; Variants (Merge overlapping, Insert interval); Three signature problems (LC 56, LC 57); Common misconceptions
study.depth: Read the Meeting-rooms-II archetype too; practise it on AlgoMaster below.

study.title: Sweep line archetypes
study.locator: The decision; Variants (1D event sweep); Variants side-by-side
study.depth: Read only the 1D event sweep variant; skyline and rectangle area are recognition only.

focus: Sort by start, walk left to right, keep one running merged interval; the overlap test is s <= last.end under LC 56's closed intervals. Sorting dominates at \(O(n \log n)\) with \(O(n)\) output.

Insert skips the sort: the input is already sorted and non-overlapping, so one pass splices the before part, the widened overlap and the after part in \(O(n)\). Re-sorting throws the precondition away for an extra \(\log\) factor.

The sweep tie-break follows the convention: half-open [s,e) processes ends before starts; closed [s,e] flips it. On [[7,10],[10,11]], ends-first counts 1 (correct for half-open) while starts-first double-counts the boundary.
The verb picks the state: collapse asks for a running interval, a new range asks for a widened newInterval, concurrency asks for a min-heap of end times or a +1/-1 balance counter.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement merge and insert. Merge [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]] must give [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]], and touching [1,3],[3,5] must merge to [[1,5]]. Insert [2,5] into [[1,3],[6,9]] must give [[1,5],[6,9]]. Implement the +1/-1 event sweep with ends-before-starts; on [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]] it must report maximum concurrency 2. Differential-test merge against a brute-force pairwise-collapse loop on random interval lists.
traps: Merging with < instead of <= on closed intervals. Touching endpoints [1,3],[3,5] overlap under LC 56's convention and must merge.
Using the sweep's \(O(N \log N)\) default as a law. Bounded coordinate ranges admit a difference array at \(O(N + R)\); the sort is the default, not the law.
Keeping the whole active set when a scalar suffices. Event counting needs one balance counter, not a heap; match the structure to what the question asks at each \(x\).

selfTest.q: Prove the merge walk never splits two overlapping intervals.
selfTest.a: Sorted by start, the walk keeps the running interval with the maximum end so far. Any interval with start <= running end overlaps it and widens it further; an interval with start > running end overlaps nothing later either, since later starts are even larger. Each emission is therefore maximal.

selfTest.q: Why is insert \(O(n)\) while merge is \(O(n \log n)\)?
selfTest.a: Insert's input is sorted and non-overlapping, so one linear splice (before, widened overlap, after) suffices. Merge must establish the order first, and comparison sorting costs \(O(n \log n)\).

selfTest.q: Under the half-open convention, why do ends sort before starts at equal coordinates?
selfTest.a: At \(x=10\), [7,10) has already ended while [10,11) begins; processing the -1 first keeps the count at 1. Starts-first would briefly count 2 and double-count the shared boundary.

selfTest.q: What changes if intervals arrive as an unbounded stream?
selfTest.a: If meetings arrive in start order, a min-heap of active end times (pop while top <= start) processes them online in \(O(n \log n)\) time with \(O(n)\) state. If they arrive in arbitrary order, no single pass works: keep an ordered map of +1/-1 events, or a segment tree over bounded coordinates, and update the maximum as events land.
